_comment: Intimacy & Relationship Experience Mapping. Christine, 2026-11-11.
NOT A QUESTIONNAIRE. These are themes the Narrative agent recognises in an ordinary
Brain Dump. Nobody opens KRYteria and says 'I would like to discuss emotional
intimacy now.' They write a messy paragraph about last night, and the agent works
out that the subject is emotional vulnerability rather than punctuality.
A THEME IS NOT A CRITERION. Criteria are the user's, created by the user, assessed
against evidence. A theme is a topic label on an entry: what this was ABOUT. The
agent may recognise 'reciprocity and initiative' in an entry from somebody who has
no reciprocity criterion at all, and that is the point — it is how the app notices
what a person keeps writing about before they have named it.
A THEME IS NOT A JUDGEMENT. Recognising 'sexual consideration and mutual
satisfaction' says the entry touched that subject. It says nothing about whether
anybody behaved well, and nothing about the person being written about.
AND A THEME IS NEVER THE SAFETY MECHANISM. `boundaries-and-consent` is a topic, not
a concern. The Safety Layer runs CONCURRENTLY with Narrative on the raw text and
does not read this file, is not gated on it, and does not wait for it. If theme
recognition ever became the route into safety handling, a missed label would become
a missed disclosure. See the roster note in the rules file.
Sensitive themes are flagged. That flag drives presentation — never a notification
preview, never a surfaced label the user did not ask to see — not whether the theme
is recognised.

themes.label: Physical attraction and sexual chemistry
themes.about: Whether the writer is drawn to the other person physically, and whether that is mutual or changing.
sounds_like: I'm not as into him as I thought
the chemistry was unreal
I don't feel anything when he touches me
themes.not_this: Do not use for an entry that merely mentions how somebody looked. The theme is the writer's experience of attraction, not a description.

themes.label: Affection and physical comfort
themes.about: Non-sexual physical closeness: whether it is present, wanted, comfortable, or withheld.
sounds_like: he never just holds my hand
I felt myself pull away
it's the only time I feel settled
themes.not_this: Distinct from attraction. Somebody can want more affection and less sex, or the reverse.

themes.label: Sexual consideration and mutual satisfaction
themes.about: Whether sex is attentive and mutual — whether the writer's experience is being considered.
sounds_like: it's always about what he wants
he actually asked what I liked
I stopped saying anything about it
themes.not_this: NOT the same as consent. An encounter can be fully consensual and entirely one-sided. Do not reach for boundaries-and-consent because the subject is sex.

themes.label: Emotional intimacy and vulnerability
themes.about: Whether either person lets the other see something real, and what happens when they do.
sounds_like: I told him about my dad and he changed the subject
he opened up for the first time
I don't think he actually knows me
themes.not_this: Not merely talking a lot. The theme is exposure and what it met.

themes.label: Feeling desired, appreciated, and respected
themes.about: How the writer experiences being regarded by the other person.
sounds_like: I feel like an option
he told his friends about my promotion
I don't think he finds me attractive anymore
themes.not_this: This is the writer's felt experience. It is an emotional_reaction, not a finding about the other person's regard.

themes.label: Comfort expressing needs
themes.about: Whether the writer can say what they want, and what it costs them to try.
sounds_like: I didn't want to make it a thing
I finally told him and he was fine about it
it's easier to just not bring it up
themes.not_this: Recognise the difficulty without characterising why. 'It's easier not to bring it up' may be habit, conflict-avoidance, or something more serious — the theme does not decide which.

themes.label: Reciprocity and initiative
themes.about: Who reaches out, who plans, who carries the relationship — and whether that is balanced.
sounds_like: I'm always the one texting first
he planned the whole weekend
if I stopped trying I think it would just end
themes.not_this: A single instance is not an imbalance. The theme marks the subject; the record decides whether there is a pattern.

themes.label: Relationship expectations and commitment
themes.about: What each person thinks this is, and whether those answers match.
sounds_like: we've never actually defined it
he said he's not looking for anything serious
I don't know if I'm allowed to call him my boyfriend
themes.not_this: Never imply which expectation is correct. A person wanting something casual and a person wanting something serious are both fine; the mismatch is the subject.

themes.label: Communication preferences
themes.about: How each person wants to stay in contact, and the friction between those styles.
sounds_like: he takes a day to answer a text
everything is great in person, the texting is driving me insane
he wants to call, I'd rather write
themes.not_this: A different texting style is not evidence of disinterest. Keep the preference separate from what the writer concluded from it.

themes.label: Boundaries and consent
themes.about: Whether a stated limit was heard and respected — in any domain, not only sex.
sounds_like: I said I didn't want to and he kept asking
I told him not to show up unannounced
he respected it straight away, which surprised me
themes.not_this: RECOGNISING THIS THEME IS NOT A SAFETY RESPONSE AND MUST NEVER BE TREATED AS ONE. The Safety Layer runs concurrently on the raw text, independently of themes and of the selected profile. A boundary respected without fuss is this theme too — the label is a subject, not an alarm.
